vc1.summary: The tea ceremony space was far and away the most beloved feature — a cozy, social anchor that people wished was bigger.
notes: One attendee summed up the holy trinity of Vibecamp as "talks, titties, and teahouse" — in that order.
Several people adored the tea house but worried it wouldn't scale, suggesting more cozy nooks if the event grows.
The teahouse-slash-cuddle-space was described as an absolute necessity — and the main request was simply: make it bigger.

vc1.summary: The cabin system gave people a built-in social home base — "default friends" to anchor an overwhelming experience.
notes: Multiple attendees described their cabin as a "Schelling point for friendship" — a reassuring default crew amid the beautiful chaos of hundreds of strangers.
Cabin selection was singled out as one of the most valuable parts of the event, letting people bond in smaller groups first.
One person loved having a built-in ingroup within the ingroup — a cozy nest of "default friends" to retreat to.

vc1.summary: The single most common complaint: two days was not nearly enough. Respondents overwhelmingly wanted 4+ days.
notes: Respondents practically begged for more days — starting Wednesday or Thursday instead of Friday was a common refrain.
Several people lobbied for 4–7 days minimum, with one dreamily suggesting a full week.
One attendee's entire feedback, in all caps: the event needed MORE DAYS.

vc1.summary: Dance events were among the most popular activities, generating powerful shared experiences and pure joy.
notes: Aella's "Descent into Dance Hell" was a particular standout that attendees raved about.
People wanted even more dancing — classes, jam sessions, and at least one person floated the idea of a masquerade ball.
Structured group activities that broke down social barriers — circling, jam sessions, group exercise — were praised as intimacy accelerators.

vc1.summary: Shared cabins with 14 people, noise, wind, and terrible beds made sleep a real struggle for many.
notes: Multiple people reported the beds were genuinely terrible — sleep deprivation apparently sapped Saturday party energy across the board.
Between the tiny bunks, flapping walls, and temperature swings, getting decent sleep in the cabins was described as a real feat.
A perpetual catch-22: someone in the cabin was always napping, making it awkward to hang out, get ready, or exist at normal volume.

vc1.summary: Name badges with Twitter handles and profile pictures were a breakthrough — making it trivially easy to connect online identities to real people.
notes: Attendees were thrilled by badges featuring Twitter handles and profile pictures — a surprisingly delightful touch.
The badges solved the "I know your avatar but not your face" problem, making it effortless to connect online personas to actual humans.
Several people credited the badge system as a crucial icebreaker for finding and remembering people all weekend.

vc1.summary: The presence of teenagers alongside drug use and nudity raised serious safety concerns about the event's future.
notes: One attendee noted how alarmingly easy it was to encounter drugs and nudity, recounting a teenager nearly getting a drug sourcing tutorial before anyone noticed.
Several people warned that a single scandal involving minors and adult activity could permanently destroy Vibecamp's reputation.
The bluntest version of a widely shared sentiment: teenagers and topless dance parties simply should not coexist.

vc1.summary: The most cherished moments were unplanned — blanket forts, impromptu dance parties, campfire conversations at 2 AM.
notes: Attendees treasured the unplanned magic — impromptu cabin dance parties, spontaneous blanket fort construction, the usual.
One person described blissfully wandering the campsite, striking up conversations with strangers, and reveling in the unscripted goodness of it all.
Multiple respondents praised the organic way people naturally flowed into shared vibes without any scheduling involved.

vc1.summary: Camp cafeteria food was widely panned, and rigid mealtimes clashed with the freeform nature of the event.
notes: Attendees yearned for a venue that would let them, say, make midnight waffles for each other after dancing — the food rules felt stifling.
One person with dietary restrictions was frustrated that their needs were ignored despite explicitly offering to self-organize.
The cafeteria food inspired the kind of reaction best expressed as a weary sigh in multiple languages.

vc1.summary: Even at the very first event, the community chemistry was undeniable — and some connections were life-changing.
notes: One attendee casually reported meeting the person who felt like their future spouse — which they considered the best possible outcome of any event, ever.
Several people described the event as a risk that paid off handsomely, with great new connections as the reward.
The pervading atmosphere of curiosity and kindness was singled out as the thing most worth preserving as the event evolves.

vc2.summary: The overwhelming highlight: finally putting faces to Twitter handles. The transition from online to IRL was electric.
notes: Attendees noted that knowing everyone was somehow connected online made approaching strangers in person dramatically easier.
Returning attendees loved the layered experience — meeting new mutuals while reconnecting with people from the previous year.
One person described the arc of the weekend: intimate sessions with fascinating people, then by Saturday night, being recognized and greeted by long-admired online friends.

vc2.summary: Attendees described a deep, sometimes overwhelming sense of belonging — many felt they'd found their tribe for the first time.
notes: One attendee from a place without many kindred spirits described Vibecamp as a sacred reminder that they're not alone in the world.
Someone calculated they have chemistry with roughly 1 in 30,000 people — and estimated that 30% of Vibecamp attendees fell into that magical sliver.
Multiple people described it as a place where they could finally stop masking — their autism, their curiosity, their weirdness all welcome.

vc2.summary: The heavily male-skewed attendance was a persistent complaint — it affected social dynamics, dating culture, and comfort for women.
notes: The male-heavy ratio was widely lamented, with one attendee noting that the average guy mostly just wanted to talk about himself.
Women attendees reported that the lack of safety features sometimes made it harder to form new connections.
Queer women in particular felt invisible, with one noting their demographic seemed to barely exist at the event.

vc2.summary: Many felt the heavy emphasis on dating shows and romance created an uncomfortable singles-bar atmosphere.
notes: Multiple attendees felt the dating programming was waaaaay overdone and wished it would be dialed back significantly.
The heavy emphasis on sex and dating was described as creepy by some, compounded by perceived celebrity entitlement.
One attendee delivered a withering mathematical observation: the gender ratio simply did not support that much dating content.

vc2.summary: Moving to Camp Ramblewood dramatically improved the experience — the cabins, showers, and intimate layout were all praised.
notes: Ramblewood's spacious cabins with in-unit showers were a massive upgrade — attendees said everything felt more intimate and accessible than Camp Champions.
The longer schedule created a sense of social and temporal abundance, replacing the frantic energy of VC1.
Thoughtfully designed spaces were credited with deepening friendships — the architecture itself was doing social engineering.

vc2.summary: The quality of conversation was unlike anything in normal life — deep, substantive, and effortless with strangers.
notes: Attendees marveled at being able to sit down with random people and immediately talk about substantial topics — something that, as one put it, rarely happens with normies.
The simple act of strangers inviting you into their conversations was cited as a highlight unto itself.
One person poetically described the interstitial conversations between people the universe seemed to have conspired to introduce.

vc2.summary: Newcomers without existing social connections often felt isolated, describing a painful divide between insiders and outsiders.
notes: Solo attendees reported that arriving without a crew made things lonelier — the event was clearly more fun for those with a built-in social home base.
One person felt things got cliquey after day one, though they charitably blamed their own autism/ADHD as a contributing factor.
The first couple of days before personal connections formed left some newcomers wandering and feeling adrift.

vc2.summary: The lack of working internet, confusing app, poor signage, and no physical schedules made finding events genuinely difficult.
notes: Figuring out what was happening and where was a persistent challenge — especially for the hardy souls sleeping rough in the woods without a phone.
Without reliable mobile data or wifi, attendees who hadn't prearranged meetups found it painfully slow to locate anyone.
The solution was presented as a clear ultimatum: offline-capable app, stable internet, or a physical schedule. Pick at least one.

vc2.summary: People used Vibecamp as a space to experiment with identity, gain life insights, and return home with concrete plans for change.
notes: One person called it a "playground for how to be" and left with 3–4 concrete things they wanted to change about their life.
For semi-anonymous accounts, Vibecamp transformed Twitter from an experience machine into a world of real people with actual faces.
Several attendees stressed how vital it was for adults to have fun that isn't reading the news and doing cardio at the gym.

vc2.summary: Many noticed a tangible shift in energy as the event progressed — people visibly relaxed and opened up.
notes: Multiple people noticed a palpable vibe shift from Thursday to Friday — everyone seemed to collectively exhale and relax.
Attendees reported opening up emotionally in ways they'd never done before, forging what felt like potential lifelong friendships.
One person described the strategy: build a safe base with existing friends first, then use that energy to explore and meet strangers.

vc2.summary: Coming without a crew was the hard mode — and the on-ramps that worked were the small ones: a randomly assigned cabin that clicked, a tent village, the low-key pre- and post-parties.
notes: One attendee's randomly assigned five-person cabin became a chill home base; they connected with three of the four strangers and called it the best thing about the weekend.
A first-timer credited their tent village with breaking the ice on day one — it became the core group they branched out from to meet everyone else.
Several people said the pre-camp meetups and after-parties were where friendships actually started: smaller, lower stakes, easier to talk.

vc2.summary: The sharpest safety feedback in Vibecamp's history: people wanted a visible safety team, a first-aid station, marked water, and straight talk about drugs — especially with kids on site.
notes: Someone needed medical attention at an off hour and nobody could tell whether there was medical staff to call — several respondents asked for a dedicated medic.
Drinking water was hard to find after the dining hall locked at night; one attendee watched a dozen thirsty people try the door and give up.
Multiple people asked for harm-reduction information and a clear line on drugs, with parents in particular saying the current ambiguity wasn't tenable.

vibeclipse.summary: Watching a total solar eclipse surrounded by hundreds of kindred spirits created an almost spiritual shared experience.
notes: One attendee apologetically admitted that the actual eclipse was simply too magical for any human activity to compete with.
People described celebrating planetary power as a collective — meeting kind, open strangers while the sky went dark.
Several attendees embraced the chance to go full woo, building ceremony around the eclipse and getting swept up in the mystic.

vibeclipse.summary: For many — especially returning attendees — Vibeclipse was the event where they finally felt they'd found their tribe.
notes: One returning attendee said it took three Vibecamps to finally open up to strangers — but when it happened, it felt life-changing.
Someone felt enough tribal potential at Vibeclipse that they immediately signed up for VC3 the moment they got home.
Multiple people described the relief of finding a pocket of "their people" and realizing they weren't alone in their thoughts and interests.

vibeclipse.summary: Conversations went deep immediately — the shared cultural context eliminated the usual social warmup period.
notes: One self-described skeptic admitted they'd heard people rave about Vibecamp conversation quality and thought it was dumb — then experienced it firsthand and conceded it was real.
Attendees noted that small talk was practically abolished; when it did appear, it signaled goodbye rather than hello.
People described feeling surrounded by intensely alive humans and opening up about things they'd never told anyone before.

vibeclipse.summary: Newcomers repeatedly described bouncing off closed friend groups — a problem that grew as the community matured.
notes: Newcomers reported that some established groups weren't looking to expand, making attempts to connect feel chilly.
One person took full responsibility but still felt that many groups seemed cliquish and uninterested in new faces.
At least one attendee frankly said they didn't feel like they belonged at all — a stark contrast to their experience at similar events.

vibeclipse.summary: With lighter programming than VC2, organic interactions flourished — boredom actually became productive.
notes: One person described letting go of all expectations and watching everything transform into serendipity.
A self-described instigator thrived in the low-structure environment — with everyone bored and waiting for someone to start something, creation came easily.
Attendees reported layers upon layers of social disinhibition building throughout the event with their friends.

vibeclipse.summary: Spiritual and ceremonial elements — particularly the midnight procession and shamanic dance — were unexpected highlights.
notes: Attendees praised the ecstatic dance party and midnight procession for adding a spiritual dimension that many hadn't expected to find.
The Midnight Procession was widely described as having kicked all sorts of ass.
For some, the event was fundamentally about healing and learning to forge deeper connections with other people.

vibeclipse.summary: The food tent was hot, uncomfortable, and the food quality was a clear downgrade from Camp Ramblewood.
notes: The cafeteria was described in near-biblical terms of suffering — hellish atmosphere, terrible lighting.
The food tent was sweltering and uncomfortable, with one attendee noting their butt hurt from the lack of decent seating.
Protein options were so scarce that at least one person was grateful they'd had the foresight to pack their own.

vibeclipse.summary: Attendees described experiences of radical openness and vulnerability that changed how they see themselves.
notes: One person described feeling like a flower slowly turning to face the sun for the first time — and even if it's gone, now they know what it's like.
Several attendees had the same revelation: there was a better way to live than what they'd been doing, and they'd finally found it.
A former commune resident who'd been missing communal life for years said Vibeclipse gave them a much-needed moment of feeling connected again.

vibeclipse.summary: The smaller size (~200 vs ~500) created an intimacy some loved but others felt was too sparse for critical social mass.
notes: Fans of the smaller size loved constantly bumping into people — the density made socializing feel natural and effortless.
Others gently noted that the headcount was less than ideal, though they were quick to frame it as a very minor complaint.
The smaller crowd amplified feelings of belonging and mutual goodwill — everyone felt relatable.

vibeclipse.summary: Multiple attendees described Vibeclipse as an existence proof that life could be warmer and more connected.
notes: One attendee summed it up simply: the event was a reminder that the universe is kind.
People described Vibeclipse as being fundamentally about radical expression and the acceptance of social eccentricity.
For those actively seeking better community in their lives, Vibeclipse served as valuable practice in building satisfying relationships.

vc3.summary: Returning attendees described VC3 not as an event but as a homecoming — the community had reached a critical mass of belonging.
notes: A self-described "Twitter nobody" who'd shown up to VC2 clueless said that by VC3, the moment they stepped off the bus it felt like home.
Returning attendees described leaving with hearts full to the brim and minds awash in possibilities.
After multiple events and local meetups, the network had grown deep enough that some attendees never felt alienated for a moment.

vc3.summary: The cozy social spaces had been iterated into their ideal form — the tea house and coffee house were the undisputed social anchors.
notes: Attendees praised the curation of the teahouse and hangout spaces as perfectly conducive to quality social connection.
The tea house at medium capacity was described as always amazing — the Goldilocks zone of coziness.
The coffee house joined the teahouse as a social anchor, paired with long conversations with delightfully strange people.

vc3.summary: Dance events matured into a defining feature — Dancehole, Buddhi's DJ sets, and dance workshops drew passionate crowds.
notes: Buddhi's DJ set was singled out with an enthusiasm that could only be expressed in all caps.
The dance programming had matured into a core draw alongside reconnecting with friends and running one's own events.
The DJ sets were widely praised as incredible, matched by the quality of conversation partners between dances.

vc3.summary: The attendee-organized programming model hit its stride — creative, weird, ambitious events flourished.
notes: The prevailing "You Can Just Do Things" attitude meant people could bounce freely from situation to situation.
Attendees who showed up and created their own spaces and events were celebrated as the event's secret ingredient.
One memorable highlight: declaring your entire deal while being sprayed with a hose in front of a cheering crowd at the pool.

vc3.summary: Double-booked venues, a glitchy app, no wifi, and unfindable locations frustrated attendees trying to participate.
notes: WiFi issues made the schedule inaccessible for many, leaving them wandering and feeling like they were interrupting things.
Events listed at vague locations like "Activity Field" were nearly impossible to find in practice.
Event organizers were frustrated to discover their scheduled slots had been double-booked by latecomers.

vc3.summary: Constant loud music — especially the pool party — made conversation difficult for some and overwhelmed neurodivergent attendees.
notes: Daytime thumpy music made conversation and even thinking difficult — the pool party was cited as the worst offender.
Neurodivergent attendees specifically asked for lower bass levels, noting that sensory issues made the volume genuinely painful.
Some attendees felt the programming leaned too heavily into dancing, meditation, and woo, leaving them without much to do.

vc3.summary: An event where people declared their "whole deal" while being sprayed with a hose became an iconic shared memory.
notes: Bashu's hose event was repeatedly named as a favorite — praised for its amazing host, amazing concept, and committed participants.
The format was simple and glorious: declare your whole deal to the crowd while being blasted with a hose.
It earned its place in the pantheon alongside the pool party, Dancehole, and Buddhi's set as a defining VC3 moment.

vc3.summary: The social norms had evolved to the point where people could share anything without fear of being judged.
notes: Attendees described deeply personal conversations with both friends and strangers, with zero sense of anything being weird or risky.
The abundance of social opportunities meant that if an event or a person didn't click, you could just move on and try again.
Fleeting moments of genuine belonging were described as extremely nice — understated but deeply felt.

vc3.summary: Despite returning to Ramblewood, wayfinding remained a major pain point — people couldn't find "Activity Field" or event locations.
notes: Locations like "Activity Field" and "Indoor Eatery and Tablespace" remained notoriously unfindable for many attendees.
Better maps, better signage, and better use of the big top were all repeatedly requested improvements.
A simple suggestion kept coming up: post the schedule at each location so people know they're in the right place.

vc3.summary: VC3 marked the moment people realized Vibecamp had become something deeper — a community built on shared values, not shared interests.
notes: One attendee observed that Vibecamp was the first community they'd joined that was purely based on shared values rather than shared interests.
People described fellow attendees as the best people on the Internet — the kindest, most thoughtful, most like themselves.
The event was characterized as a giant energetic conflagration of happiness, caring, positivity, and "yes and" energy all in one space.

vc3.summary: A year after VC2's safety asks, people noticed the fixes: a medic on site, water stations, lights in the fields, and more volunteers looking out for newcomers.
notes: One returning attendee said they felt safer than the previous year, and named exactly why — the on-site medic, the water stations, and the lit fields.
A first-timer who knew nobody described volunteers and campers alike making sure they felt included.
Physical safety scored 4.9 out of 5 — the highest-rated question of the year, and it has stayed there since.

vc3.summary: Women described a weekend of mostly respectful interactions and an exhausting volume of them — and asked for a way to signal "not here to date."
notes: Several women said nearly everyone was respectful when they asked for space, but constantly having to set that boundary was tiring in itself.
One attendee distinguished conversations that treated her as a person from ones that treated her as a prospect, and wished for a visible signal to deflect the latter.
A male attendee said the ratio had been honestly framed to him in advance — so he came to hang out, not to find a soulmate, and had a great time.

vc4.summary: By the fourth Vibecamp, the norm of radical welcome had become the defining quality — strangers could walk up to anyone and be embraced.
notes: Attendees marveled at being able to walk up to literally anyone and be welcomed into their conversation — it felt genuinely safe.
One person noted that hearing strangers say "Hey! Come sit with us" is rare in the world, but blessedly common at Vibecamp.
People who usually struggle to find others on the same wavelength reported that at VC4, everyone was on it.

vc4.summary: Multiple attendees met romantic partners — the vibes-to-romance pipeline was operating at peak efficiency.
notes: At least one attendee reported meeting the person they plan to marry. Casual.
Another person MET A GUY AND REALLY HIT IT OFF (their all-caps enthusiasm, not ours).
One attendee was pleasantly surprised when the weekend yielded not just new friends but an intense romantic escapade.

vc4.summary: A preview of a musical adaptation of Scott Alexander's novel became one of the most talked-about moments of the event.
notes: Group artistic events remained the main draw for many, and this year Unsong was the crown jewel.
The Solstice concert and Unsong preview were paired with the simpler pleasure of dozing in a hammock in the shade.
The Unsong musical was enthusiastically praised across multiple survey responses.

vc4.summary: A heat wave during the event made outdoor participation genuinely difficult and was the most common complaint.
notes: The heat was especially brutal for attendees with health issues, making basic participation genuinely difficult.
Access to air conditioning or even powerful fans was desperately requested — THE HEAT was the number one complaint.
One attendee memorably described the air as hot soup while they attempted to staple an endless pile of flowers to the ceiling.

vc4.summary: An unauthorized documentary crew sparked serious backlash — people felt their ability to "fly their freak flag" was threatened.
notes: The sentiment on filming was blunt: keep it out, let people fly their freak flag without worrying about cameras.
Privacy-conscious attendees warned that being photographed and posted could have very real consequences for them.
Being filmed without permission was cited as a straightforward violation of the event's trust.

vc4.summary: Attendees described the event as a pilgrimage, a homecoming, or a place where they could finally be fully themselves.
notes: Multiple attendees simply said: it feels like being home.
The event was described as coming home to one's people — a convergence of safety, community, and connection.
One respondent was too emotionally overwhelmed to even answer with specifics, calling it an enormously positive and life-changing experience.

vc4.summary: Despite the welcoming culture, first-timers still reported status hierarchies and difficulty breaking into existing groups.
notes: Some attendees detected emerging cliquishness and status hierarchies that could feel intimidating for newcomers.
High-follower-count attendees were described as sometimes feeling unreachable, even though the observer suspected this was partly a "me problem."
There were calls for more structured icebreaking, especially at the start — the reason we loved summer camp as kids was the structure that helped us get to know each other.

vc4.summary: By VC4, attendee-run programming had evolved into delightfully unhinged territory — jousting, waterboarding, combat sports.
notes: One attendee's highlight reel included: circling for the first time, jousting, getting waterboarded, and kissing a cutie. Just normal weekend stuff.
Ill-considered combat sports, an anti-outgroup rally, and enthusiastic strangers infodumping about their strange interests were all cited approvingly.
The sheer quirkiness of the attendee-organized programming was a widely celebrated feature.

vc4.summary: Questions around filming, nudity near children, and bathroom/shower policies revealed growing pains in community norms.
notes: The tacit acceptance of nudity and sexual activity alongside the presence of children was flagged as deeply uncomfortable by some.
The lack of any single-sex shower or bathroom option was raised as a concern — one attendee argued that having zero such options was exclusionary, not inclusive.
Changes to the media consent policy raised alarm bells for attendees who valued Vibecamp as a space where they could safely be themselves.

vc4.summary: People described VC4 as a transformative experience — a space where they discovered new parts of themselves.
notes: Attendees described feeling more secure and comfortable than they ever had, discovering new parts of themselves in the process.
One person said they reconnected with someone they used to be — someone they hadn't been in touch with in a long time — and got to say hi to that younger version of themselves.
The event was described as a sneak preview of what all of life should be like, a north star to orient toward the rest of the year.

vc4.summary: Wayfinding was VC4's quiet frustration: map names that didn't match the ground, spaces missing from the map entirely, and a map that lived on a phone with no reception.
notes: Several people described hunting for bathrooms and water stations during tent setup because they were unmarked on the app map and reception was too poor to dig through emails — the ask: accurately marked paper maps.
The names of spaces baffled people: "Side Room 1" turned out to be up by the big top, and nobody was quite sure where "activity field" was.
Requests converged on physical signage, "You Are Here" maps at the major venues, more lighting on dark paths, and a calendar that groups events by location and time.

vc4.summary: Families reported a camp that worked for them: babysitting on Friday and Saturday nights, a kids' swim hour, and a parent community that felt fully part of the event.
notes: Parents praised the babysitting on both party nights and said it let them have the adult version of Vibecamp too.
One parent said integrating families during the day shows people on the fence that you can "really have it all" at Vibecamp.
Kids-adjacent moments — a petting zoo, a swing set built as an event — were listed among the highlights by people without children too.

vc4.summary: Every year a few people conclude Vibecamp isn't for them — more party than they wanted, or a subculture they didn't share — and most say so with real grace.
notes: One attendee wrote that every logistical need was met and everyone around them was having an amazing time; the community just might not be for them, and that's okay.
Another felt an unspoken culture with a high barrier to entry — everyone was kind, but being out of touch with the online scene held them back.
A few found the energy more "party" than in previous years, and wanted the quieter, conversation-first version of camp.

vc5.summary: The walk-up-to-anyone culture is now simply how Vibecamp works — people described a high-trust weekend where social barriers melted on contact.
notes: One attendee said they could enter almost any conversation and be welcomed — and they tested it, repeatedly.
Someone called it "opposite world": a whole weekend where weird nerds are the default group, so everyone fits in by definition.
Multiple people reported zero social anxiety all weekend — a refreshing difference from day-to-day life, credited to the camp-wide high-openness norm.

vc5.summary: For many, VC5 delivered the headline feeling: belonging somewhere, some for the first time in their lives.
notes: One attendee put it simply: it meant feeling like they belong somewhere — something they had never felt before.
Another described finally not feeling like a weirdo or an outsider in a group: "what I wanted summer camp to be like as a kid."
A returning attendee described serving tea at the teahouse and getting emotional over it — this year they got to be the person their VC2 self didn't dare aspire to become.

vc5.summary: Running your own event was repeatedly named the single best part — the programming model where attendees make the thing is now the thing.
notes: Several people said hosting their own event was "absolutely the highlight" — the attendee-run format made it feel like a big party with friends instead of a formal conference.
One person said running their own event left them feeling more alive than they usually do — and that the emotional risks they took were met with more care than they could describe.
One person praised the freewheeling ability of attendees to spin up events on a whim as the engine of the whole experience.

vc5.summary: The solstice sing-along, emo night, folk and partner dances, and a certain tree net were the moments people kept naming.
notes: The summer solstice sing-along came up again and again as a peak collective moment, alongside a transcendent midnight mass.
Partner and folk dancing earned devoted fans — including as an unexpectedly effective way to meet people across the gender ratio.
One attendee's entire answer to "best aspects": tree net, tree net, tree net.

vc5.theme: Conversations You Can't Get Anywhere Else
vc5.summary: The no-small-talk culture held strong — strangers went deep immediately, and people left with their year's best conversations.
notes: One person said they can start talking to a random person at Vibecamp and have a better conversation than they could ever dream of having in a bar.
An attendee described it as a shortcut to high-intensity sociality without needing to build trust over months.
"I can't believe how much good conversation I had this year" was a representative sentiment, not an outlier.

vc5.summary: The most consistent criticism: newcomers — especially those not active on Twitter — struggled to break into established groups, and mealtimes were the loneliest.
notes: Several first-timers described "new kid at school" feelings, most acutely at the dining hall when everyone around them seemed to already have a group.
One non-Twitter attendee found it hard to integrate anywhere, since the social network largely assumes you arrive with mutuals.
Concrete fixes were volunteered: veteran-newcomer buddy pairings, early mingling events for the non-extremely-online, and signals for who's open to being approached.

vc5.summary: The teahouse remains the heart of camp — and it's now so central that it's overcrowded, doubling as music venue and makeout lounge when people need it as a quiet refuge.
notes: Attendees asked, nearly verbatim: "we need like… two more teahouses" — more chill spaces to lay around and hang out.
People seeking a calm place to recover from emotional overwhelm found the teahouse already occupied by experimental jazz.
Suggestions included a dedicated quiet/recovery space, separate from the teahouse's social gravity.

vc5.theme: Dinner at Seven Was a Crime
vc5.summary: Food logistics drew the sharpest practical feedback: dinner came too late, the gap from lunch was brutal, and between-meal options were scarce.
notes: Multiple attendees independently lobbied for dinner at 5–6pm — 7–9pm is prime event time, and the lunch-to-dinner gap left people crashing.
A proposed fix: an official mid-afternoon "tea time" snack break so people refuel and socialize on the same schedule.
Vegetarian dinner options and late-night vegan food got specific thumbs-down, though breakfasts, lunches — and this year's food overall — earned surprised praise from others.

vc5.summary: June in Maryland asserted itself: overheated tents and outdoor sessions, mosquitoes, and tick anxiety were the top venue complaints.
notes: Several people had to duck out of outdoor sessions from overheating and asked for more indoor or shaded programming space.
Air-conditioned cabins were treasured by those who had them — and requested by everyone who didn't.
One attendee proposed tick-hostile landscaping: gravel paths and short-trimmed grass.

vc5.summary: Four years after VC1's all-caps plea for MORE DAYS, the request stands: one more day is the consensus ask.
notes: "Too short! Another day would have been perfect" — a sentiment echoed across many responses.
One attendee with disabilities explained that it takes days just to get settled, and camp ends right as they're ready to dive in.
Notably, several pushed back on a full week: the magic partly comes from intensity, and one extra day — maybe two — is the sweet spot.

vc5.summary: Finding out what's happening still depends on wifi that only sometimes exists. The schedule tool keeps improving — and the asks keep coming: an offline schedule, a physical events board, better filters.
notes: Multiple people asked for a way to know what's on without a phone: an offline schedule, or a central events board with a chalkboard for last-minute additions.
The schedule tool earned real praise ("gets better every year") alongside specific bug reports and feature requests — filtering by venue or "what's on in the next hour," and clearer start times.
All-weekend joke events crowding the calendar made it harder to use; one suggestion was individualized calendar feeds.

vc5.summary: The opening-ceremony consent exercise, the media policy, and the incident-reporting rundown were named as reasons people felt safe enough to be fully themselves.
notes: One attendee said the media policy encouraged them to be fully themselves, and singled out the consent exercise and incident-reporting briefing as what made the space feel safe.
People described a high-trust setting where strangers could assert a boundary kindly — or be trusted not to steal from an unattended bag.
The counterpoint: a few found the "no taking photos without consent" rule too strict, and would rather it applied to posting than to taking.

vc5.summary: First-timers who found a foothold fastest had a job, a guide, or both — and several asked us to make that the default rather than the lucky exception.
notes: A first-timer who volunteered for teahouse setup said having a "job" and meeting a few people before the doors opened gave them an instant place.

One newcomer credited a friend who acted as "training wheels" — and wondered aloud about the first-timers who arrived without one, suggesting veterans pair up with them to answer questions and make introductions.
Someone new to the whole online scene said people were happy to fill them in on the culture — they just had to ask.
